scenes.visual: Title card 'The Price of Cold' fades in over a cartoon lab chamber with a mouse inside and tubes for air in and out, 16:9. Same colour map as the first film: heat made, M = ORANGE; heat gained, G = YELLOW; dry leak = BLUE outlet whose WIDTH is conductance, C; evaporation, E = PALE CYAN; body temperature, Tb = tank fill level with a RED thermometer; air temperature, Ta = GREY dashed line; the gap = GREY bar. Right half of the frame holds empty axes: vertical 'heat made (M)' in ORANGE, horizontal 'air temperature (Ta)', warm air on the right, cold on the left. Curves are computed from M = C × (Tb − Ta) with invented mouse-like values and labelled 'computed, invented values'; anything else is labelled 'schematic'. Numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Put a mouse in a chamber and cool the air, one step at a time. What happens to the heat it makes? And why does nothing happen at first?
scenes.visual: The chamber's GREY air thermometer steps down, click by click. The mouse sits still inside. On the empty axes a question mark hovers over the ORANGE axis. Question card: 'Cooler air: when does the mouse pay?'
scenes.narration: Put a mouse in a chamber and cool the air, one step at a time. What happens to the heat it makes? And why does nothing happen at first?

scenes.tts: The first film drew the body as a tank. Heat made flows in through the orange tap. Heat leaks out through a blue outlet whose width can change. Now we watch what holding the level costs.
scenes.visual: Left half: the mouse's tank from the first film returns, ORANGE tap in, BLUE outlet out, RED thermometer at the level. The YELLOW tap appears, then switches off, labelled 'no sun in the chamber'; the PALE CYAN outlet dims, labelled 'evaporation left out (model)'.
scenes.narration: The first film drew the body as a tank. Heat made flows in through the orange tap. Heat leaks out through a blue outlet whose width can change. Now we watch what holding the level costs.

scenes.tts: In this model, we leave out sun and evaporation. So heat made must match the blue leak. We read heat made from the oxygen the mouse uses. At each step, we plot one orange point.
scenes.visual: A small gauge on the chamber's air outlet labelled 'oxygen used → heat made'. Each time the air steps down, an ORANGE dot drops onto the axes at the matching air temperature. Balance beam overlay: ORANGE 'M' on one side, BLUE 'C × (Tb − Ta)' on the other, level.
scenes.narration: In this model, we leave out sun and evaporation. So heat made must match the blue leak. We read heat made from the oxygen the mouse uses. At each step, we plot one orange point.

scenes.tts: At first, the orange points stay flat. The mouse holds its temperature without making extra heat. Instead, it narrows the blue outlet. Skin vessels close, and fur lifts.
scenes.visual: As the GREY air line falls on the tank and the gap bar lengthens, the BLUE outlet narrows step by step: cartoon skin vessels pinch, fur fluffs. The ORANGE tap stays the same. On the axes, ORANGE dots line up flat.
scenes.narration: At first, the orange points stay flat. The mouse holds its temperature without making extra heat. Instead, it narrows the blue outlet. Skin vessels close, and fur lifts.

scenes.tts: This flat stretch is the thermo-neutral zone. The resting rate along it is the basal metabolic rate, measured at rest and not digesting.
scenes.caption: This flat stretch is the thermoneutral zone. The resting rate along it is the basal metabolic rate, measured at rest and not digesting.
scenes.visual: A shaded band under the flat dots, labelled 'thermoneutral zone'. A horizontal ORANGE line through the dots labelled 'basal metabolic rate (BMR)'.
scenes.narration: This flat stretch is the thermoneutral zone. The resting rate along it is the basal metabolic rate, measured at rest and not digesting.

scenes.tts: But the outlet can only get so narrow. At the lower critical temperature, our model mouse reaches its narrowest outlet. Its conductance is at its minimum.
scenes.visual: The BLUE outlet narrows to a clamp icon labelled 'model: C at its minimum'. On the axes, a vertical tick at the left edge of the flat band labelled 'lower critical temperature'.
scenes.narration: But the outlet can only get so narrow. At the lower critical temperature, our model mouse reaches its narrowest outlet. Its conductance is at its minimum.

scenes.tts: Below that, the model holds the outlet at its minimum. Now only the orange tap can answer. Each degree colder adds the same extra heat. So the points climb in a straight line.
scenes.visual: The air keeps stepping down; the GREY gap bar keeps lengthening; the BLUE outflow speeds up; the ORANGE tap opens wider each step. On the axes, ORANGE dots now climb in a straight line toward the cold side, labelled 'model: C held at minimum'. A small step triangle on the line: one degree across, 'C watts' up.
scenes.narration: Below that, the model holds the outlet at its minimum. Now only the orange tap can answer. Each degree colder adds the same extra heat. So the points climb in a straight line.

scenes.tts: Extend that line toward warmer air, and it reaches zero at body temperature. That zero is only arithmetic. A living animal always makes some heat.
scenes.visual: A dashed ORANGE extension runs from the climbing line, under the flat band, down to the horizontal axis, meeting it at a tick labelled 'Ta = Tb'. Label on the dashed part: 'extrapolation only'. The flat BMR line stays above it.
scenes.narration: Extend that line toward warmer air, and it reaches zero at body temperature. That zero is only arithmetic. A living animal always makes some heat.

scenes.tts: Per Scholander, Laurence Irving and colleagues measured curves like this. They plotted resting heat made against air temperature, for mammals from the arctic and from the tropics.
scenes.visual: Credit text: 'Scholander, Irving and colleagues, 1950'. Two cartoon icons slide in: a thick-furred arctic fox in snow and a thinly furred tropical mammal among leaves. Their tanks appear small beside the axes, same ORANGE tap size, labelled 'same basal rate and body temperature (assumed)'.
scenes.narration: Per Scholander, Laurence Irving and colleagues measured curves like this. They plotted resting heat made against air temperature, for mammals from the arctic and from the tropics.

scenes.tts: Now give an animal thicker fur, with the same basal rate and body temperature. Does the bend move to colder air, or to warmer air?
scenes.visual: The fox's tank gets a thick fur wrap; its BLUE outlet floor clamps narrower than the mouse's. On the axes, a blank second curve outline with a question mark at the bend. Question card: 'Thicker fur: bend colder or warmer?'
scenes.narration: Now give an animal thicker fur, with the same basal rate and body temperature. Does the bend move to colder air, or to warmer air?

scenes.visual: Question card holds; a small timer ring fills.

scenes.tts: Colder. A narrower outlet can carry the basal heat away only across a bigger gap. And below the bend, the climb is shallower.
scenes.visual: A computed curve for a well-insulated animal draws in: the same flat BMR line, a bend much farther left, and a cold limb with a gentler slope; its dashed extension meets the axis at the same 'Ta = Tb' tick. The GREY gap bar on the fox's tank is drawn much longer at its bend. Label: 'computed, invented values'.
scenes.narration: Colder. A narrower outlet can carry the basal heat away only across a bigger gap. And below the bend, the climb is shallower.

scenes.tts: That is the pattern they found. Thick-furred arctic mammals stayed on their flat line into far colder air than tropical ones. The difference lay mainly in insulation, not in a higher basal rate.
scenes.visual: Overlay of three computed curves sharing one flat BMR line and one zero point at Ta = Tb: the tropical curve bends close to body temperature and climbs steeply; the mouse in the middle; the arctic curve bends far to the cold side and climbs gently. Labels 'tropical', 'mouse', 'arctic'. Text: 'difference: mainly insulation (C), not basal rate'.
scenes.narration: That is the pattern they found. Thick-furred arctic mammals stayed on their flat line into far colder air than tropical ones. The difference lay mainly in insulation, not in a higher basal rate.

scenes.tts: So the curve is the heat balance, plotted against the air. Conductance sets where the bend falls, and how steeply the cost climbs below it.
scenes.visual: The three curves dim except their bends and slopes, which pulse in BLUE. The balance 'M = C × (Tb − Ta)' fades in above the cold limbs. The tank beside the axes shows its BLUE outlet width tied by a thin line to each curve's slope.
scenes.narration: So the curve is the heat balance, plotted against the air. Conductance sets where the bend falls, and how steeply the cost climbs below it.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Line: 'Conductance sets where cold starts to cost, and how much.'
